```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)

# Must match EXPERIMENT.id in experiment.js, and the --experiment you passed to the export.
# Phase 2 runs under its own id, so its data never mix with Phase 1's.
experiment_id        <- "patil2018-pilot-a"
experiment_id_phase2 <- "patil2018-phase2"

# Minimum test trials for a session to be analysed. A full session has 484 (242 scenes + 242
# objects). PILOT ONLY: lowered to 48 so shortened ?n=24 runs on localhost can be analysed.
# Set back to 484 before the final data collection.
min_test_trials <- 48
```

```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures. Replace these with your original study's
# values, and say in a comment exactly where in the paper each one comes from.
#
# Patil & Duncan (2018), Experiment 1, N = 32 analysed (Method, p. 46).
# Results, p. 48: corrected associative-memory accuracy was 8.23 percentage points higher
# after an "old" judgment than after a "new" judgment on the preceding trial,
# 95% CI [4.10, 12.36], F(1, 31) = 13.88, p = .001, partial eta squared = .31.
original_n <- 32
original <- tibble(
  N        = original_n,
  estimate = 0.0823,   # old minus new, as a proportion
  ci_low   = 0.0410,
  ci_high  = 0.1236,
  F        = 13.88,
  df       = original_n - 1,
  p        = 0.001,
  pes      = 0.31
)

# Standardized paired effect for the power analysis: with 1 numerator df, F = t^2,
# so d_z = t / sqrt(N) = sqrt(F) / sqrt(N), about 0.66. (The reported CI implies a slightly
# larger t, about 4.1; the F is used because it is the test the paper reports.)
original_dz <- sqrt(original$F) / sqrt(original_n)

# Per-condition means for the side-by-side figure. The paper gives no table of means, so the
# "new" bar is read off Fig. 2a (p. 49, approximate) and the "old" bar is that plus the reported
# 8.23-point difference. Error bars in Fig. 2a are the SE of the difference between conditions
# (Morey, 2008); that SE is recovered here from the reported 95% CI: half-width / t(.975, 31).
original_se_diff <- (original$ci_high - original$ci_low) / 2 / qt(0.975, original_n - 1)
original_means <- tibble(
  prev_judgment = c("new", "old"),
  mean          = c(0.355, 0.355 + original$estimate),
  se            = original_se_diff,
  N             = original_n
)
```

# Key statistics

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

One row per study for the key comparison: the original, your Phase 1
replication, and your Phase 2 extension. The table fills itself in from
the data as each phase is exported, using the analysis code below (open
"Show the analysis code"), which is shared by both phases so they are
analysed identically. Edit that code once, here, to match your design
and preregistered exclusion rule. On the scientific-extension track, the
Phase 2 row reports the new comparison: adapt its code and say so in the
caption.
:::

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  complete <- participants |> filter(completed)

  # Exclusion rule (participant level), following Patil & Duncan (2018), Exp. 1 (p. 46):
  #   - reported prior participation in a similar study ("Yes"; "Not sure" is kept),
  #   - reported drowsiness "Throughout most of the study",
  # plus two checks on the session itself:
  #   - fewer than `min_test_trials` test trials (set at the top; 484 = a full session),
  #   - no response to any test trial (what a device without a keyboard produces).
  post <- trials |>
    filter(task == "post_study") |>
    mutate(resp = map(response, ~ fromJSON(.x))) |>
    transmute(participant_id,
              prior_participation = map_chr(resp, ~ as.character(.x$prior_participation %||% NA)),
              drowsiness          = map_chr(resp, ~ as.character(.x$drowsiness %||% NA)))
  ret <- trials |>
    filter(task == "retrieval") |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(n_retrieval = n(),
              n_responded = sum(!as.logical(timed_out)),
              .groups = "drop")
  checked <- complete |>
    left_join(ret, by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(post, by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(excl_short       = is.na(n_retrieval) | n_retrieval < min_test_trials,
           excl_no_response = !excl_short & n_responded == 0,
           excl_prior       = prior_participation %in% "Yes",
           excl_drowsy      = drowsiness %in% "Throughout most of the study",
           excluded         = excl_short | excl_no_response | excl_prior | excl_drowsy)
  keep <- checked |> filter(!excluded)

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, checked = checked, keep = keep,
       n_no_response = sum(checked$excl_no_response))
}

# Per participant x preceding judgment x category: corrected associative-memory accuracy and
# d', computed as in Patil & Duncan (2018), Data analysis (pp. 47-48).
#   - Test trials only; timed-out trials and trials with no preceding judgment in the same
#     block (first trial after a break, or the previous trial timed out) are dropped.
#   - Response priming: trials whose correct word equals the previous response are removed.
#   - Associative memory: old images called old. Corrected accuracy = p(correct word) -
#     p(wrong word) / 2. "Old, can't remember" (F) responses count in the denominator only.
#   - Item memory (d'): trials without a correct association. Hits = old images called old,
#     false alarms = new images called old, with the log-linear correction (add 0.5 to
#     counts and 1 to totals) so rates of 0 or 1 stay finite.
memory_words <- c("ancient", "plain", "safe")
memory_cells <- function(d) {
  t <- d$trials |>
    filter(task == "retrieval", participant_id %in% d$keep$participant_id) |>
    mutate(is_old = as.logical(is_old), timed_out = as.logical(timed_out)) |>
    filter(!timed_out, prev_judgment %in% c("old", "new")) |>
    filter(!coalesce(studied_word == prev_response_label, FALSE)) |>
    mutate(assoc_hit = is_old & judgment == "old" & response_label == studied_word,
           assoc_fa  = is_old & judgment == "old" & response_label %in% memory_words &
                         response_label != studied_word)
  t |>
    group_by(participant_id, prev_judgment, category) |>
    summarise(n_assoc   = sum(is_old & judgment == "old"),
              assoc_acc = if (n_assoc > 0) (sum(assoc_hit) - sum(assoc_fa) / 2) / n_assoc else NA_real_,
              n_old     = sum(is_old & !assoc_hit),
              n_new     = sum(!is_old),
              hit_rate  = (sum(is_old & !assoc_hit & judgment == "old") + 0.5) / (n_old + 1),
              fa_rate   = (sum(!is_old & judgment == "old") + 0.5) / (n_new + 1),
              dprime    = qnorm(hit_rate) - qnorm(fa_rate),
              .groups = "drop")
}

# Each participant's accuracy after "old" and after "new" judgments, averaged over category.
# Only participants with every cell (2 judgments x 2 categories) are kept, as in the ANOVA.
by_participant <- function(cells, dv = "assoc_acc") {
  cells |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    filter(n() == 4, !any(is.na(.data[[dv]]))) |>
    group_by(participant_id, prev_judgment) |>
    summarise(value = mean(.data[[dv]]), .groups = "drop") |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = prev_judgment, values_from = value)
}

# The key statistic: mean old-minus-new difference in corrected associative accuracy, with a
# 95% CI and the paired t test. With one numerator df this is the main effect of preceding
# judgment in the 2 x 2 ANOVA (F = t^2), so it has the same columns as `original`.
# NULL when no participant has data in every cell.
diff_ci <- function(cells) {
  w <- by_participant(cells)
  if (nrow(w) == 0) return(NULL)
  diffs <- w$old - w$new
  N <- length(diffs)
  if (N < 2) {
    return(tibble(N = N, estimate = mean(diffs), ci_low = NA_real_, ci_high = NA_real_,
                  F = NA_real_, df = N - 1, p = NA_real_, pes = NA_real_))
  }
  tt <- t.test(diffs)
  F  <- unname(tt$statistic)^2
  tibble(N = N, estimate = mean(diffs), ci_low = tt$conf.int[1], ci_high = tt$conf.int[2],
         F = F, df = N - 1, p = tt$p.value, pes = F / (F + N - 1))
}

# Condition means for the figure, with the same error bar as Fig. 2a: the SE of the
# old-minus-new difference (Morey, 2008), drawn on both bars.
condition_means <- function(cells) {
  w <- by_participant(cells)
  if (nrow(w) == 0) return(NULL)
  se <- if (nrow(w) > 1) sd(w$old - w$new) / sqrt(nrow(w)) else NA_real_
  tibble(prev_judgment = c("new", "old"), mean = c(mean(w$new), mean(w$old)),
         se = se, N = nrow(w))
}

# Side-by-side figure: any number of studies on the same axes, in the order given. Each is
# a tibble from condition_means() (or `original_means`); NULL or empty studies are skipped.
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           prev_judgment = factor(prev_judgment, levels = c("new", "old"),
                                  labels = c("\u201cNew\u201d", "\u201cOld\u201d")),
           label = sprintf("n = %d", N))
  fills <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.8)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = prev_judgment, y = mean, fill = Study)) +
    geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.75) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), position = dodge, width = 0.2,
                  na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_text(aes(y = 0.02, label = label), position = dodge, vjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "white") +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(min(0, df$mean - df$se, na.rm = TRUE), 1)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills) +
    labs(x = "Preceding judgment", y = "Corrected associative-memory accuracy", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
# Each row is a one-row tibble with the same columns as `original` (N, estimate, ci_low,
# ci_high, F, df, p, pes), from diff_ci() under Key statistics. Statistics that need at least
# two analysed participants show as a dash until there are two.
fmt_row <- function(study, r, have = FALSE) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "",
                  `Effect (old − new)` = if (have) "not enough data yet" else "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", F = "", p = "", `ηp²` = ""))
  }
  dash <- function(x, txt) if (is.na(x)) "—" else txt
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Effect (old − new)` = sprintf("%.2f points", 100 * r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = dash(r$ci_low, sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", 100 * r$ci_low, 100 * r$ci_high)),
         F = dash(r$F, sprintf("F(1, %d) = %.2f", as.integer(r$df), r$F)),
         p = dash(r$p, format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)),
         `ηp²` = dash(r$pes, sprintf("%.2f", r$pes)))
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", original),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) diff_ci(memory_cells(phase1)), have_data),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) diff_ci(memory_cells(phase2)), have_phase2)
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrlllrr",
               caption = "Key comparison: corrected associative-memory accuracy after an \"old\" judgment minus after a \"new\" judgment on the preceding trial, in percentage points.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

### Justification

In this paper, Patil and Duncan found that recent exposure to
familiarity selectively improved associative memory (Experiment 1), and
that this effect decayed over seconds (Experiment 2). During my PhD, I
plan to study the development of different memory subprocesses,
including pattern completion and separation, so this paper will help me
better understand how these processes are studied in adults, as well as
how this type of data is analyzed, for example, using a Signal Detection
Theory framework to assess memory accuracy.

### Procedure and Challenges

This replication involved creating two online experiments using the same
stimuli from the original paper, which the authors made available on the
Open Science Framework. The stimuli consisted of 484 images on a white
background. Unlike the original study, I collected data online through
Prolific. One challenge I faced was obtaining quality data from an
online sample, which required implementing features that prevented bots
from completing the task.

### Statistical tests

Separate 2 (preceding judgment: old vs. new) × 2 (stimulus: object vs.
scene) repeated measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were used to
analyze corrected associative-memory accuracy, response time on trials
on which associative memory was correct, and d′.Paired-samples t tests
(two-tailed) were used to examine simple effects. For pairwise
comparisons, t tests were conducted with Bonferroni correction. Two
generalized mixed-effects models were estimated with an unstructured
covariance matrix to control for response time on the preceding trial
and preceding trial type, respectively.

### Extension

Because one of my concerns is that the length of this study (\~50
minutes) will affect data quality, I would like to run it with less
trials to see if an effect can be detected. Also, inspired by a
suggestion from a TA, I could also test for differences between age
groups.

## Methods

### Power analysis

The estimate reported in the paper is **F(1, 31) = 13.88**, and the
effect size is **ηp2 = 0.31**. I chose to maintain the original sample
size mainly due to budget constraints. This experiment takes around \~50
minutes to be completed, and I am planning to play \$10/h. Therefore,
increasing the sample size to reach half of the reported effect size
would require a budget outside of the scope of the class.

```{r}
#| label: power
# Within-participant design: the key test is a paired comparison (the 1-df main effect of
# preceding judgment), so power is for a paired t test at the original d_z.
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- power.t.test(delta = original_dz, sd = 1, power = pw, sig.level = 0.05,
                    type = "paired")$n
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n_total = ceiling(n))
})

# 2.5 times the original sample (Simonsohn, 2015). A single number now: the inline text
# below still indexes two frames (two_and_half[2] will show NA until it is rewritten).
two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original_n)

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N participants"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Sample needed to detect the original effect (%.2f points, d_z = %.2f from F(1, %d) = %.2f), paired, two-sided alpha = .05.",
               100 * original$estimate, original_dz, original$df, original$F))
```

For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample would be
`r two_and_half[1]` in the gain frame and `r two_and_half[2]` in the
loss frame (`r sum(two_and_half)` in total).

### Planned sample

The planned sample size is: 35 adult participants (18 and older) who are
currently living in the US and are fluent in English.

### Materials

The stimuli will be the same as in the original experimental design:

*"Stimuli consisted of colored images of 242 natural indoor and outdoor
scenes and 242 common objects (484 images total), along with three words
(“ancient,” “plain,” “safe”)"*

The authors published the original stimuli online, however, due to
maintenance of the OSF website, I am currently using **a different set
of images** of scenes and objects from the Brady Lab at UCLA and the
Konkle lab at Harvard (Brady, Konkle, Alvarez & Oliva, 2008). As soon as
I gain access to the orignal stimuli, the images will be replaced.

Links to the provisional images:

-   Konkle images set: https://konklab.fas.harvard.edu/#
-   Brady lab images set: https://bradylab.ucsd.edu/stimuli.html

### Procedure

The procedure will be close to the original experiment, with the main
difference that the current replication will be held online.

The total study is divided into

1.  Consent form
2.  Images preloading. Participant waits for a few seconds without
    taking action.
3.  Welcome page. Brief explanation of the study.
4.  Demographic information
5.  Experiment 5.1 Study phase 5.2 Retrieval phase
6.  Post study questions: strategy, drowsiness.
7.  Feedback: question about instructions clarity.
8.  Debrief.

The task takes \~50 minutes to complete.

The design and timing will follow the original paper:

"*The experiment consisted of an encoding session in which participants
associated each image with one of the three words and a retrieval test
that simultaneously assessed associative memory for the words and item
memory for the images.*

*Encoding session. During each trial in the encoding session, an
image-word pair was displayed on the screen for 3 s. Images were trial
unique, and each image was pseudo-randomly paired with one of the three
words, such that all three words appeared an equal number of times
across the experiment. Participants were asked to vividly imagine a
scenario in which the word could describe the image to encourage deep
processing of image-word pairs. After the pair disappeared, participants
had 1.5 s to rate the imagined scenario on a 4-point continuous scale on
the keyboard, using “h” (very vivid), “j,” “k,” and “l” (not vivid at
all). A fixation cross was presented at the center of the screen for 1 s
before each trial. A post study debriefing session revealed that all
participants’ memory encoding strategies were consistent with the
instructions. Participants were informed before the encoding session
that their memory would be assessed. The encoding session was split into
eight 3-min blocks. Half the blocks consisted of scene-word pairs, and
the remaining blocks consisted of object-word pairs. Scene and object
blocks were presented in a counterbalanced alternating order.*

*Retrieval session. During the memory test, we assessed participants’
item and associative memory simultaneously. Critically, we manipulated
whether participants made each memory decision after an unrelated
familiar or novel image. During each retrieval trial, an image was shown
on the screen for 2 s. Participants were asked to indicate whether the
image was new (by pressing the “d” key) or old, in which case they were
asked to recall the word associated with it in the encoding session (by
pressing the “j,” “k,” or “l” keys, which corresponded with “ancient,”
“plain,” and “safe,” respectively). They were asked to press the “f” key
if they thought that an image was old but were unable to recall the
associated word (associative skip). Note that these response options
allowed us to assess participants’ item and associative memory with a
single response. The response window was intentionally short, consistent
with past research (Duncan et al., 2012), so that (a) memory judgments
were made before the mnemonic processing bias from the preceding trial
dissipated and (b) the bias from the preceding trial would not be
overcome with sufficient processing time. A central fixation cross was
presented during a 1-s interstimulus interval (ISI).*

*The retrieval session was split into four 6-min blocks. Half of the
images presented during the memory test had been previously studied
during the encoding session, while the remaining were novel. Critically,
scene and object images alternated during the memory test. This reduced
the possibility of consecutive old images semantically priming each
other, because consecutive images always belonged to different stimulus
categories and were, thus, studied during different encoding blocks.
Stimulus presentation was predetermined such that no more than four new
stimuli appeared consecutively and the transition probability between
seeing old and new images was .50.*

![](images/original-figure.png){width="547"}

### Analysis plan

The planned exclusion criteria are:

-   Trials in which participants switched tabs (browser interactions).
-   Trials that were preceded by an excluded trial based on tab
    switches.
-   At the participant level, I will exclude participants with more than
    10% of test trials affected by the trial-level rule.

The main statistical test will be the same stated in the paper:
*"Separate 2 (preceding judgment: old vs. new) × 2 (stimulus: object vs.
scene) repeated measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were used to
analyze corrected associative-memory accuracy, response time on trials
on which associative memory was correct, and d′. Paired-samples t tests
(two-tailed) were used to examine simple effects."*

The analysis is aimed at revealing a main effect of preceding judgment
(old vs. new) on corrected associative memory accuracy. Specifically,
accuracy is expected to be higher when the preceding trial was
identified as old.

### Differences from the original study

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Sample | College students from Toronto | Adults recruited on Prolific | Possibly. Framing effects have been found in both student and general samples, but their size varies across populations. |
| Setting | In lab experiment | Online, unsupervised, on the participant's own computer | Possibly. This is a long study that probably benefits from the controlled environment of a laboratory setting. |
| Wording | The exact wording is not available online | Based on the description given in the paper | Unlikely. The instructions are essentially the same |

### Methods addendum (post data collection)

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Leave this section out of the version you preregister. After data
collection, report the actual sample and any deviation from the plan
above.
:::

```{r}
#| label: funnel
#| eval: !expr have_data
funnel_levels <- c("Started", "Completed", "Passed exclusion criteria")
bind_rows(
  participants |> mutate(step = "Started"),
  complete     |> mutate(step = "Completed"),
  keep         |> mutate(step = "Passed exclusion criteria")
) |>
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = funnel_levels)) |>
  count(step, .drop = FALSE) |>
  rename(Step = step, Participants = n) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Participants at each step. The design is within-subjects, so there are no conditions to compare attrition across.")

# Why completed sessions were excluded (a session can meet more than one criterion).
phase1$checked |>
  summarise(!!sprintf("Shortened session (< %d test trials)", min_test_trials) := sum(excl_short),
            `No response to any test trial`        = sum(excl_no_response),
            `Prior participation`                   = sum(excl_prior),
            `Drowsy throughout`                     = sum(excl_drowsy)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Reason", values_to = "Completed sessions excluded") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Exclusions among completed sessions.")
```

### Data preparation

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
# 2 (preceding judgment: old vs new) x 2 (stimulus: object vs scene) repeated-measures ANOVAs
# on corrected associative-memory accuracy (confirmatory) and d', as in the original.
cells <- memory_cells(phase1)
rm_anova <- function(cells, dv) {
  complete_ids <- by_participant(cells, dv)$participant_id
  dat <- cells |> filter(participant_id %in% complete_ids)
  if (length(complete_ids) < 2) {
    message("ANOVA on ", dv, " not run: ", length(complete_ids),
            " participant(s) with data in all four cells; it needs at least two.")
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  afex::aov_ez(id = "participant_id", dv = dv, data = dat,
               within = c("prev_judgment", "category"), anova_table = list(es = "pes"))
}

cells |>
  group_by(`Preceding judgment` = prev_judgment, Category = category) |>
  summarise(Participants = n_distinct(participant_id),
            `Corrected assoc. accuracy` = round(mean(assoc_acc, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
            `d′` = round(mean(dprime, na.rm = TRUE), 2), .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Cell means across analysed participants (before requiring complete cells).")

rm_anova(cells, "assoc_acc")
rm_anova(cells, "dprime")
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test
is significant. Compare the replication estimate and its interval with
the original: does the interval exclude zero, and does it include the
original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original,
or a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original
effect, are both informative and should be reported as such
(Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- original
rep  <- diff_ci(cells)

if (!is.null(rep) && !is.na(rep$ci_low)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Difference (old − new)` = sprintf("%.2f points", 100 * estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", 100 * ci_low, 100 * ci_high),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: corrected associative-memory accuracy after an \"old\" minus after a \"new\" judgment.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: it needs at least two analysed participants with data in every cell.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep) && !is.na(rep$ci_low)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$estimate >= rep$ci_low & orig$estimate <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.2f points. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    100 * orig$estimate))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and
your replication side by side.** It is the single most informative thing
in a replication report: a reader can see at a glance whether the effect
came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in
roughly this order of preference:

1.  **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary
    statistics (means or proportions, with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in
    the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot them on
    the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.

2.  **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or
    it is in an open repository, using exactly the same plotting code as
    for your own data.

3.  **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is
    possible. Save a screenshot of it, for example as
    `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out in
    columns:

    ```` markdown
    ::: {layout-ncol=2}
    ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

    ```{{r}}
    # your replication plot here
    ```
    :::
    ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and
error-bar meaning for both panels, label which is which, and cite the
source of the original values or figure in the caption. If the original
reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Corrected associative-memory accuracy after a \"new\" vs an \"old\" judgment on the preceding trial, original study (Patil & Duncan, 2018, Exp. 1: the \"new\" bar read off Fig. 2a, the \"old\" bar from the reported 8.23-point difference) and Phase 1 replication. Error bars are the standard error of the difference between conditions (Morey, 2008), as in the original; for the original it is recovered from the reported 95% CI."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
comparison_plot(Original = original_means, `Phase 1: replication` = condition_means(cells))
```

# Phase 2: Extension

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance: choosing your extension

Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas. In brief:

-   **By default the extension is a best-practices modification of your
    Phase 1 experiment.** If your replication did not succeed, it is a
    **rescue**: address the plausible reasons for the failure. If it did
    succeed, it is an **upgrade**: make the estimate more precise.
    Typical changes are better or more reliable measurement, more
    trials, a within-participant design where that is legitimate,
    comprehension and manipulation checks, clearer instructions, or a
    larger or better-targeted sample.
-   **If your scientific extension pitch was approved at Milestone 3 and
    your replication succeeded, propose that instead:** the original
    conditions rerun unchanged, plus the one added condition or
    manipulation, with a power analysis for the new comparison.
-   On either track you may add exploratory measures **at the end** of
    the study.
-   Every change is listed and tagged by category below; everything else
    stays identical.

State your track on the line below, and delete the others.
:::

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade / Best-practices rescue / Scientific
extension (approved at Milestone 3)

## Rationale

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs. For a rescue: what are the plausible reasons
Phase 1 did not reproduce the original result, and how does each change
address one of them? For an upgrade: where is the Phase 1 estimate least
precise or least trustworthy, and how will the changes improve it? For a
scientific extension: what question does the added condition answer, and
why does it follow from the original finding?
:::

## Changes from Phase 1

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Every change from the Phase 1 experiment, one per row, each tagged with
a category: Measurement, Trials, Design, Checks, Instructions, Sample,
Added condition (scientific track only), or Exploratory measure (end of
study only). If it is not in this table, it does not change: same
materials, wording, procedure, exclusion rule and analysis. The rows
below are examples for the demo; replace them with yours.
:::

| \# | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| 1 | Sample | 27 analysed participants | 300 analysed participants (150 per frame) | Phase 1's interval was too wide to distinguish the original effect from a much smaller one. |
| 2 | Checks | No comprehension check | After the choice, participants say how many people are at risk (600) | Confirms participants read the scenario; failures are reported, and excluded only if preregistered. |
| 3 | Exploratory measure | None | At the end: "How confident are you in your choice?" (1–7) | Exploratory only; collected after every confirmatory measure. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Justify the Phase 2 sample, and **state how you expect the estimate and
its precision to compare with Phase 1**. For an upgrade, plan the sample
around the confidence interval you want; for a rescue, around the power
to detect the original effect, or the smallest effect you would still
consider a successful replication; for a scientific extension, around
the power to detect the new comparison. Set `phase2_n_per_group` in the
code below; the table uses Phase 1's estimate if you have it and the
original's otherwise.
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
# Within-participant design: every participant is in both conditions, so this is the total
# number of analysed participants (the name is kept to match the guidance above).
phase2_n_per_group <- 150   # planned analysed participants in Phase 2

# Phase 1 statistics: a one-row tibble with the same columns as `original` (N, estimate,
# ci_low, ci_high, F, df, p, pes). NULL until your Phase 1 analysis code defines it; the
# tables then fall back to the original study.
p1_stats <- NULL

# SD of the per-participant difference: from Phase 1 if available, otherwise implied by the
# original CI (half-width = t(.975, N - 1) * SD / sqrt(N)).
sd_from_ci <- function(r) (r$ci_high - r$ci_low) / 2 / qt(0.975, r$N - 1) * sqrt(r$N)
basis <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) {
  list(sd_diff = sd_from_ci(p1_stats), dz = p1_stats$estimate / sd_from_ci(p1_stats), source = "Phase 1")
} else {
  list(sd_diff = sd_from_ci(original), dz = original_dz, source = "the original study")
}

# Expected 95% CI half-width on the paired difference with n participants.
half_width <- function(n) qt(0.975, n - 1) * basis$sd_diff / sqrt(n)
power_at <- function(n, dz) {
  tryCatch(power.t.test(n = n, delta = dz, sd = 1, sig.level = 0.05, type = "paired")$power,
           error = function(e) NA)
}

rows <- tibble(
  Study = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$N, phase2_n_per_group),
  `95% CI half-width` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("±%.2f points", 100 * (p1_stats$ci_high - p1_stats$ci_low) / 2),
                          sprintf("±%.2f points (expected)", 100 * half_width(phase2_n_per_group)))
)
knitr::kable(rows, caption = sprintf("Precision of the key estimate, Phase 2 expected values based on %s.", basis$source))

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: %.2f points (d_z = %.2f)", 100 * original$estimate, original_dz),
                         if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: %.2f points (d_z = %.2f)", 100 * p1_stats$estimate, basis$dz),
                         sprintf("Half the original: %.2f points (d_z = %.2f)", 50 * original$estimate, original_dz / 2)),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, original_dz),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_at(phase2_n_per_group, basis$dz),
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, original_dz / 2)
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 key test (paired) at N = %d, two-sided alpha = .05.", phase2_n_per_group))
```
